meta.purpose: Curated skill procedures injected as the 'skills' arm of the harder-v2 context-injection experiment.
meta.provenance: Hand-authored general engineering procedure. Contains no corpus patches, no reference solutions, and no code from any benchmark task.

shapes.listener-identity: Cleanup only works by identity. The registration and the removal must name the exact same function object; a fresh closure is a different object and removes nothing.
shapes.error-aggregation: Decide the aggregate outcome for every-input-failed, some-failed and none-failed before writing code, collect all outcomes without short-circuiting, and throw a collected error only when nothing succeeded.
shapes.recency-ordering: Separate capacity enforcement from recency bookkeeping, refresh recency on every read and write, and evict the single least-recent entry after the refresh, not before.
shapes.timer-cancellation: Cancellation must clear the exact handle returned by the scheduling call, be idempotent, and reset any correlated bookkeeping so a later call cannot observe stale state.
shapes.graph-traversal-memo: Identity-keyed memoisation must register a container before descending into it so that a reference back to an ancestor resolves inside the copy instead of recursing again.
shapes.concurrency-gate: Model the limit as a running-count plus a pending queue, and release capacity on both success and failure paths so a rejected unit cannot permanently consume a slot.
shapes.merge-semantics: Merge is type-directed: scalars replace, arrays combine, nested containers recurse. A generic shallow assign does none of this.
shapes.backpressure-wait: Under saturation the caller's promise must still settle. Hold pending resolvers in a queue and admit work through one FIFO drain path shared by enqueue and completion.
shapes.retry-schedule: Express the delay as a formula over base and attempt index computed per call, so concurrent retries cannot share mutable schedule state.
shapes.transition-validation: Permitted transitions belong in one lookup table, consulted by a single decision point, and a rejected transition must leave observable state unchanged.

procedure: Note the registration and the removal sites. A removal call only succeeds when it receives the same function object that was registered.
Reuse one named reference for both registration and removal, or keep a registry mapping an owner key to the exact callbacks it registered.
When a listener closes over per-call state, tie the registry entry to that call and delete it on the same path that removes the listener, so entries cannot accumulate.
Verify by asserting the listener count is stable across repeated register/remove cycles, not merely that no error was thrown.
traps: Removing with fn.bind(this) or an inline arrow expression: both create a new identity.
Checking that the removal call happened rather than that the internal registry shrank.

procedure: Enumerate the required outcomes first: all inputs fail, some fail, none fail. Write down the expected return for each.
Collect every outcome without short-circuiting: await all work, then partition into fulfilled and rejected.
When every input rejected, throw the collected error (AggregateError, or the single error when only one exists).
Otherwise return the fulfilled values; keep rejections out of the successful return value.
Never let a rejection escape an await inside a loop that is meant to continue, and never let a catch turn 'all failed' into a silent success.
traps: await inside try/catch that rethrows per item, or that swallows the only rejection.
Returning early on the first failure, so partial successes are lost.

procedure: Separate the two responsibilities: capacity enforcement and recency bookkeeping.
Make every read and write path refresh recency. A read that does not refresh order yields FIFO, not LRU.
Enforce capacity after the recency update, evicting exactly one least-recent entry per over-capacity insert.
Assert that the container's size stays bounded; growth past capacity means eviction is not running or picks the wrong end.
Verify with an interleaved sequence: fill to capacity, read one key, insert again, then assert the read key survived and the untouched key was evicted.
traps: Tracking recency with a counter but comparing with >= or <=, so eviction removes the wrong entry.
Refreshing recency only in set(), leaving get() to look like a no-op for ordering.

procedure: Identify what the cancel path must stop: a scheduled callback, an in-flight loop, or both.
Clear the exact handle produced by the scheduling call, and make cancel safe to call more than once.
Reset the correlated bookkeeping (handle, deadline, pending flag) so a later invocation cannot read stale state.
Decide the post-cancel contract for the wrapped call: it must not fire, and it must not leave a caller waiting for a result that will never come.
Verify by cancelling and then waiting past the original delay, asserting the callback never ran.
traps: Clearing a handle variable that was reassigned by a later schedule call.
Setting a cancelled boolean without clearing the timer, leaving the callback pending.

procedure: Characterise the input domain: nested containers, and containers that reference themselves.
Add an identity-keyed memo (WeakMap for objects, Set for a visited path) recording containers already seen or already copied.
Check the memo before descending, and register the new container before visiting its children.
On re-entry return the already-produced copy, so internal references point into the copy rather than the original.
Verify with a self-referencing object and assert both termination and that the copy's back-reference resolves inside the copy.
traps: Memoising only primitive values.
Registering the container after recursion, so the cycle is still re-entered once.

procedure: State the invariant precisely: at most N units of work are in flight at any instant.
Model it with a running counter plus a queue of pending starters.
Start work through a single drain path: while capacity remains and work is pending, take one item and run it.
Release capacity on completion of every unit, including rejections, and attempt another drain each time.
Verify by submitting more work than the limit, observing the maximum concurrency reached, and asserting every unit eventually ran.
traps: Releasing capacity only on the success path, which leaks slots on failure.
Draining only on enqueue, so the queue stalls when completions outpace submissions.

procedure: Write down what merge means per type: scalars overwrite, arrays combine, nested objects recurse, order preserved left-then-right.
Find the actual collision: a generic assign/copy path that treats containers like scalars, so the right side replaces the left.
Special-case containers before the scalar path: recurse for objects, combine for arrays.
Do not mutate the inputs unless the previous behaviour did.
Verify with a key defined as a container on both sides, and assert non-conflicting keys from both sides survive.
traps: Object.assign or spread, which is shallow and replaces arrays wholesale.
Recursing into the first differing type without checking both sides are containers.

harder-v2-async-queue.classTitle: Waiting instead of rejecting under backpressure
procedure: Establish the saturation contract: the caller's promise must settle only when its work has run or definitively failed.
Replace rejection-when-full with waiting: retain the caller's resolver in a pending queue.
Admit work through one drain path so ordering is FIFO and no item is admitted twice.
Run the drain on completion as well as on enqueue, so the queue empties even when no new submission arrives.
Verify by deliberately overflowing, then asserting every submitted item ran exactly once and in order.
traps: Dropping the retained resolver, leaving the caller pending forever.
Keeping the old rejection path active as well, so overflow can still fail.

procedure: Write out the required delay sequence for attempts 0..n before implementing.
Implement the sequence as one formula over base delay and attempt index, not a chain of special cases.
Keep schedule state per call, so concurrent retries cannot share mutable delay state.
Apply jitter or caps only if the specification asks for them.
Verify by recording the delays actually used and comparing them against the expected sequence.
traps: Accumulating with delay += step (linear) when the specification asks for doubling from the base.
Reusing one mutable delay variable across attempts so the growth compounds incorrectly.

procedure: Extract the permitted transitions into data: a table keyed by current state (and event) whose values are the allowed next states.
Centralise the decision in one place: look up the table, then either advance or reject. No other path mutates state directly.
On rejection, throw with both the attempted transition and the current state in the message, and leave the state unchanged.
Treat unknown states and events as invalid rather than permissive.
Verify that a valid path advances, and that an invalid attempt throws and leaves the machine in its previous state.
traps: Mutating state before validating, so a rejected transition still changes the machine.
Validating with a permissive default (allowing anything not explicitly forbidden) which accepts unknown events.
